A long high note launched from Caroline's mouth with the full power of a drummer used to facing rock concert noise. Her clear and strong voice immediately bounced off all the cave walls, echoing many times over, creating a powerful natural reverb effect.
“DOOOOooooo….. dooooo….. dooo…. doo…” Caroline's voice echo seemed unwilling to stop, dancing in the darkness.
Everyone fell silent, stunned by Caroline's vocal power (and that cave's echo power). But the silence afterward didn't last long.
Cheep… cheep… cheep… CRIIIIIIIIIIIIIITTTTTT!!!

From the dark cave ceiling, hundreds, maybe even thousands of small black dots suddenly moved simultaneously! A colony of bats sleeping soundly, disturbed by Caroline's sudden solo concert, flew in panic in all directions! The sound of their flapping wings and their ultrasonic screams filled the cave chamber, creating total chaos.
“BATS! THEY'RE AWAKE! THEY WANT TO ATTACK! VAMPIRES!” Andrea screamed hysterically, immediately covering her head with both hands and crouching on the floor.

Sharon and Nisa reflexively ducked too. Reza and Alex tried to protect Nisa. The Presidential Security Force immediately formed a formation protecting the group, their flashlights panicking toward the ceiling. Jim? He actually looked enthusiastic. “Brilliant! An interesting phenomenon! Sound waves at certain frequencies can apparently trigger a mass defensive response in a Chiroptera colony!”

Caroline herself, the cause of that chaos, could only stand gaping in the middle of the room, her mouth still slightly open. “Uh… sorry? Is my voice that good it startled them?” she asked innocently to the guide whose face had already turned pale.

It took several minutes that felt like forever to calm the situation. The guides promptly directed the group to exit that large chamber toward a safer corridor. The bat colony slowly calmed down and sought a new perching place in darker corners of the cave.

When they finally managed to exit the cave and breathe fresh air again (which felt very relieving after the distinctive bat aroma), Andrea was still slightly trembling. “I swear, there was one bat that flew right in front of my face! I could feel the wind from its wings!”
Caroline approached Andrea with a guilty face. “Sorry, An. I didn't know my voice could wake the entire dracula army.”
“Next time if you want to do a vocal test, maybe just in the bathroom, Car,” Sharon said while patting her sister's shoulder, between amused and slightly annoyed.
Jim added, “But this is interesting data for bio-acoustic research, Caroline. Maybe your high voice has the same resonance frequency as bats' sonar system? There's scientific potential here!”

Nisa could only let out a long sigh. Today's adventure was truly beyond expectation. From the beauty of stalactites and stalagmites, to Caroline's solo concert ending with a bat invasion. It seemed there was no “normal” day when vacationing with The Corrs.

“Okay,” Nisa said finally, trying to lighten the mood. “How about this, how about we look for lunch now? I heard there's a good seafood restaurant near the port. And I promise, the menu has no fried bat.”

Nisa's joke successfully made everyone laugh with relief. The incident at Batu Cermin Cave might have been slightly tense (especially for Andrea), but once again, it became another unforgettable funny story in their journey. And Caroline? She might think twice before trying a vocal test in places with “too good” acoustics again.
11: Parting with Labuan Bajo and the luxury pinisi ship felt slightly heavy-hearted. The Corrs had begun getting used to life at sea, with the lulling wave rocking (except when Jim explained theories about undersea currents that could swallow ships) and unparalleled sunset views. However, curiosity about the next island, Sumba, which Nisa described as “Indonesia's African Savanna with a mystical touch,” was enough to reawaken their adventurous spirit.

The flight to Tambolaka or Waingapu in Sumba presented drastically different aerial views. The blue expanse of the Flores Sea slowly changed to drier land, golden-brown limestone hills, vast valleys overgrown with grassland, and occasionally visible towering unique traditional house roofs.
“Wow, this is really different from Bali or Lombok,” Sharon commented while staring out the plane window. “It feels more… ancient? More majestic?”

“Correct. Sumba is a very special island, Sharon,” Nisa answered, sitting across the aisle. “Its Marapu culture is still very strong, its nature wild but extraordinarily beautiful. And what's most famous…” Nisa deliberately left her sentence hanging.
“What? A land version dragon?” Andrea guessed, still slightly traumatized by komodos.
Nisa laughed. “No. But almost as mighty. Its horses! Sumba's Sandalwood horses.”

Upon landing and making the land journey to one of West Sumba's most authentic traditional villages (of course with escort and coordination already neatly arranged), The Corrs immediately felt a different atmosphere. Traditional houses with towering tower roofs (Uma Mbatangu), large megalithic stone graves scattered in the village yard, and villagers welcoming with friendly smiles yet still maintaining their traditional dignity.

The village head and traditional elders welcomed President Nisa's group with a simple yet solemn welcoming ceremony. There was an energetic war dance from the village youths, an offering of betel nut (which this time was politely declined by The Corrs, learning from Jim's experience nearly getting 'drunk' when trying it on another occasion), and a presentation of Sumba ikat woven cloth whose motifs were so intricate and beautiful.

“This… this is extraordinary,” Caroline whispered to Alex, her eyes not leaving the detail of the woven cloth just given to Nisa. “How can they make patterns this intricate by hand? This is the coolest handmade in the world!”

Alex tried explaining the weaving process that could take months, about natural dyes, and about the philosophical meaning behind every motif. Jim, of course, was already involved in discussion with one of the traditional elders (helped by a translator) about the Marapu belief system and its relationship with megalithic tradition.

While engrossed in admiring that traditional village's uniqueness, suddenly the sound of approaching horse hoofbeats was heard. From the village's end, a group of Sumba youths appeared riding those famous Sandalwood horses. Those horses weren't too large, but their posture was sturdy, their running fast, their coats gleaming, and their eyes looked wild and free. They ran without saddles, controlled only with simple rope by their riders who looked so merged with those mighty animals.

Andrea's eyes immediately sparkled brightly. Since childhood she had indeed loved horses, and seeing these Sumba horses looking so free and exotic, her adventurous soul (which was sometimes a bit reckless) immediately surged.

“OH MY GOD! LOOK AT THOSE HORSES! SO HANDSOME!” she shrieked, momentarily ignoring the woven cloth she was holding. She immediately jogged toward the village yard's boundary fence, her eyes not leaving the horses running showing off their might.
One golden-brown horse with a long black mane looked to very much attract Andrea's attention. That horse ran fastest, looked most spirited.

“Nisa! Reza! Look at that one!” Andrea pointed at that brown horse. “I… I want to ride that horse! May I? Just a moment! I can ride horses!” Andrea whined to Nisa, putting on her signature puppy eyes.
Nisa, who was conversing with the village head, immediately turned hearing Andrea's request. Her face changed slightly tense.

“Andrea, dear,” Nisa approached Andrea, her voice gentle but her tone firm. “These Sumba horses aren't tame ponies at an amusement park. These are racing horses, war horses in the Pasola tradition. They're wild, requiring special skill to ride, especially without a saddle.”
“But I can! When I was little I often rode ponies!” Andrea retorted, unwilling to give up. “Come on, Nisa… just a moment. I promise to be careful!”
Reza tried to mediate. “Andrea, Nisa is right. This is for your safety too. These Sandalwood horses have enormous strength. If you fall…”
“I won't fall!” Andrea cut in stubbornly. “I'm agile! Just watch!” She was even preparing to climb the boundary fence.

“Andrea Corr!” Nisa's voice this time was truly firm, without compromise. Her presidential tone came out. Andrea immediately stopped moving, slightly startled hearing Nisa's tone of voice that was rarely that firm with her. “I said no, so no. I don't want our vacation ending with you or the horse injured. Understand?”

Andrea pouted, her lips protruding several centimeters. She stared at that brown horse with a sad gaze, then looked back at Nisa with a pleading stare. But seeing Nisa's unshakeable gaze, she finally gave in.
“Yes… yes… I understand, Madam President,” she answered softly, slightly disappointed.
Sharon approached her sister, putting an arm around her shoulder. “Enough, An. We can just take photos with the horses later when they've stopped running. That's already cool enough.”
Caroline added, “Yes! Rather than Auntie Nisa having to give an apology speech to the Sumba horse king because you stressed out his horse?”

Caroline's joke successfully made Andrea smile a little. Jim, who had apparently been observing that interaction, approached and said to Andrea, “Philosophically, Andrea, your desire to conquer that wild horse might be a metaphor for humanity's desire to master nature. But sometimes, true beauty actually lies in observation and appreciation from a safe distance, not in conquest.”
Andrea only rolled her eyes hearing Jim's lecture, but she knew her brother had a point (though she wouldn't admit it).

That day, Andrea indeed didn't succeed in becoming an impromptu Sumba cowboy. But she gained a valuable lesson about appreciating local culture and her own capability limits (as well as the limits of an Indonesian President's patience). She finally settled for just taking photos with her dream brown horse (after that horse calmed down and was held by its actual rider).

The visit to that Sumba traditional village closed with lunch together with the villagers, tasting simple local dishes like grilled corn and rumpu rampe vegetables. The Corrs looked to so enjoy the sincere and warm interaction with the villagers, learning several Sumba words, and admiring the beauty of their woven cloth and traditional houses.

The charm of the Sumba traditional village, with all its cultural uniqueness and its mighty horses (which Andrea didn't succeed in conquering), left a deep impression in The Corrs' hearts. This was another side of Indonesia so different, so authentic, and so stunning. Tomorrow, they would witness one of Sumba's most iconic (and perhaps most tense) festivals: Pasola! Roughly, how hysterical would Caroline be seeing spears flying?
12: Day 15: “Flying to Kalimantan! Nisa and the Spontaneous Speech 'How to Survive in the Forest (for Beginners)' on the Plane”

Leaving Sumba with all its ancient exoticism felt like closing one chapter of an adventure book and opening a completely different new page. If Sumba was about vast savanna, wild horses, and soul-stirring traditional rituals, then Kalimantan promised adventure in the heart of dense tropical rainforest, navigating brownish rivers, and meeting directly (hopefully from a reasonable distance) with charismatic red-haired primates.

The flight to Pangkalan Bun, Central Kalimantan — the gateway to Tanjung Puting National Park — was made with a smaller but still comfortable presidential plane. As the plane took off leaving Sumba, the view changed from dry hills to endless green expanse interspersed with large rivers winding like giant snakes.
“So… we're really going to enter the forest… like in the Tarzan film?” Caroline asked from her seat, her eyes staring at the green expanse below with a mixture of amazement and slight dread.

“Not exactly like Tarzan, Caroline,” Nisa answered while smiling, closing the brief report folder she was reading. “We'll navigate the river with a comfortable klotok boat, visit an orangutan rehabilitation center, and observe wildlife in their natural habitat. This will be an extraordinary experience, but of course, there are several things we need to pay attention to.”

Nisa suddenly stood from her seat, walked to the plane aisle, and put on a slightly more serious facial expression, imitating the style of a flight attendant about to give a safety demonstration, but with a President's touch of authority (and a bit of mischief).

“Alright, VVIP passengers,” Nisa began her 'spontaneous speech,' her voice slightly more formal, making The Corrs, Reza, and Alex immediately turn with full attention (and slight amusement). “Welcome to the special 'President Nisa Airlines' flight to the heart of Kalimantan. For our comfort and safety together over the next few days in the orangutan and proboscis monkey habitat, allow me to give a brief briefing on 'How to Survive in the Forest (for Beginners, The Corrs version).'”

Andrea immediately straightened her sitting posture, her face tense. Sharon took out her notebook. Caroline prepared her phone camera, thinking this was part of the attraction. Jim listened with full analytical interest.

“First,” Nisa raised her index finger. “About Fauna. In the forest later, we might meet various types of insects. Remember the grasshopper incident in Ubud, Andrea?” Andrea nodded quickly, her face immediately alert. “Well, in Kalimantan, the insects might be a bit more… exotic. There are giant ants, rhinoceros beetles, and also… leeches.”
“LEECHES?! VAMPIRE WORMS?!” Andrea and Caroline shrieked simultaneously, their faces uniformly pale.

“Relax, relax,” Nisa hurried to calm them. “We'll wear boots and super effective anti-insect lotion specially mixed by the Palace. The possibility of being bitten by leeches is very small. But if it does happen,” Nisa stared at them one by one with a dramatic style, “don't panic! Don't pull them off forcibly! Just drip eucalyptus oil or tobacco on them, they'll let go by themselves.”
“Eucalyptus oil? Tobacco?” Sharon repeated while taking notes. “Okay, noted. Irish folk survival kit.”

“Second,” Nisa continued. “About flora. The forest is very dense. Never try to eat fruit or mushrooms we don't recognize, however beautiful their color. Remember, what's pretty isn't necessarily good.” Nisa glanced at Andrea who yesterday nearly tried frangipani flowers thinking they were candy. “And don't carelessly touch vines; who knows if that's nettle or… a snake nest?”
“SNAKES?!” This time Sharon was slightly startled, scribbling in her book in panic.

“The possibility of meeting dangerous snakes on the route we'll take is very small,” Nisa reassured (though inwardly she also prayed a little). “But the point is, look but don't touch unless the local guide says it's safe.”

“Third,” Nisa took a breath. “Most important: Orangutans. They are extraordinarily intelligent, strong, and charismatic primates. We'll visit Camp Leakey, where they usually get supplementary feeding. But remember,” Nisa stared at Andrea intently, “they are NOT cute dolls or pets. Don't try to feed them directly from your hand, however organic the banana you carry!” Andrea immediately hid her handbag which she suspected still had leftover banana from breakfast. “Don't make eye contact too long with adult male orangutans; that can be considered a challenge. And never try to… ahem… philosophize with them, Jim.”
Jim raised an eyebrow. “Why not? Maybe they have a unique perspective on deforestation from a victim's viewpoint?”

“They might, Jim,” Reza chimed in while holding back laughter. “But we don't want to risk being misunderstood and ending up as philosophical discussion material up a tree by them, especially if the topic is deforestation.”

“Fourth,” Nisa continued her speech. “Proboscis monkeys. The iconic long-nosed monkeys. They're shy, so we just observe from afar. And please,” Nisa glanced at Caroline, “don't try to imitate their sound or pose imitating their long nose for a selfie. That's impolite.” Caroline immediately lowered her phone already ready with a long-nose filter.

“Fifth,” Nisa said again. “Hydration and Health. Kalimantan's air is humid, so drink lots of water. Bring a hat, sunblock, and anti-mosquito lotion at all times. If you feel unwell, dizzy, or suddenly want to sing a yodel song for no reason, immediately report to me, Reza, Alex, or the medical team always on standby.”

“Lastly,” Nisa smiled widely. “Enjoy every moment! This is a rare opportunity to see the true wonder of Indonesia's nature. Open your eyes, open your ears, open your heart. But don't open your mouth too wide if there's a flying insect, okay?”
President Nisa's 'How to Survive in the Forest' speech closed with lively applause (and slight relieved laughter) from The Corrs.

“Okay, Madam President!” Andrea exclaimed, now looking slightly calmer (or perhaps resigned?). “I'm ready! I'll bring anti-leech lotion, anti-snake, anti-angry-orangutan, and maybe a little lucky charm from Ireland!”
“I'll try to appreciate the orangutan's perspective from a safe distance,” Jim added seriously.
“And I won't imitate the proboscis monkey's nose!” Caroline promised.
“I'll just enjoy nature's music,” Sharon said while smiling.

The plane began preparing to land at Pangkalan Bun. The Corrs' hearts beat slightly faster. The adventure in Kalimantan's wilderness would soon begin. With the 'safety speech' provisions from President Nisa, they felt slightly more prepared, though they knew surprises (and silliness) were surely already waiting at every river bend and dense foliage.
13: The sixteenth morning began not with a hotel alarm or birdsong at a luxury villa, but with the bustling noise of activity at the small port of Kumai, the main gateway to Tanjung Puting National Park. The Palace group and The Corrs, after a quick breakfast in Pangkalan Bun, were escorted to the dock where their 'vehicle' for the next few days was already waiting: a klotok boat.

For The Corrs, the words 'klotok boat' might have conjured a simple rickety wooden boat. But what awaited them was the VVIP version. A fairly large two-level wooden boat, brightly painted, with a spacious open deck on the upper level complete with cushioned rattan chairs and a dining table, plus several comfortable air-conditioned sleeping cabins on the lower deck. Though traditional in form, its facilities were clearly adjusted for special guests' comfort (and to dampen potential complaints from Andrea about insects).
“This is… a klotok?” Sharon asked slightly hesitantly while boarding the boat, comparing it with the simple klotok pictures she'd seen on the internet.
“This is the Klotok Palace Edition, Auntie Sharon,” Alex answered while grinning, having already boarded first and chosen the best spot on the upper deck. “Five-star facilities, thousand-star views!”

As soon as the boat began moving slowly leaving Kumai port and entering the Sekonyer River whose water was brownish like milk tea, the atmosphere immediately changed. The port's bustle was replaced by the silence of dense nipa forest on both sides of the river. The air felt humid and warm, filled with the aroma of wet earth and forest sounds beginning to be heard — whistles of exotic birds, monkey screams from a distance, and of course, the klotok boat's engine sound that was monotonous yet soothing (“Klotok… klotok… klotok…”).

Nisa took a long breath, feeling a tranquility different from Ubud. “Well, this is my office for the next few days,” she said while pointing toward the endless green forest before her. She had deliberately brought several work folders, thinking she could chip away a bit at state duties amid this calm atmosphere.
Reza smiled seeing Nisa's stack of folders. “Sure you can focus on work here, love? The view is too tempting.”

And indeed true. That river journey was like entering another world. Occasionally they saw large monitor lizards sunbathing at the river's edge, bright blue kingfishers darting quickly, or groups of long-tailed macaques hanging from tree branches. Every river bend presented a stunning new view.

The Corrs were transfixed. Andrea, who was initially still slightly tense from Nisa's 'forest briefing' yesterday, slowly began relaxing, enchanted by the wild natural beauty around her (though she remained alert to the potential appearance of flying leeches or anacondas). Sharon took out her sketchbook, trying to capture the river and forest atmosphere in pencil strokes.

Jim Corr? He found his favorite spot at the front deck's end. Not to passively enjoy the view, of course. He sat cross-legged, holding a thick-covered book he'd brought from Ireland. Its title? Who knows the original title, but Nisa and Reza agreed to nickname it “Jim Corr's Collection of Strange Theories Book.” That day, it seemed the chapter he was reading was about Kalimantan's endemic primates. Occasionally he would lower his book, take his binoculars (not Andrea's anti-dragon ones, but ordinary binoculars), observe the monkeys at the river's edge, then return to writing notes in his book with a seriously furrowed brow.
“What's he researching now?” Nisa whispered to Reza.

Reza peeked at the chapter title Jim was reading. “Seems like about… The Existential Quandary of the Proboscis Monkey: A Philosophical Inquiry into Nasal Morphology and Social Hierarchy,” Reza read softly. Nisa could only shake her head while holding back laughter. “Proboscis Monkey Philosophy”! Only Jim Corr might read it in the middle of Kalimantan's forest.

While Jim was immersed in the world of long-nose philosophy, Caroline felt the klotok atmosphere was too… calm. Her rock 'n roll soul needed a bit of a beat. She saw there was a small sound system in the deck's corner that the boat crew seemed to have prepared for entertainment. With permission from the boat captain (who might have slightly regretted it later), Caroline connected her phone.
And suddenly…
THUMP! THUMP! BASS!

Instead of calm nature sounds, that klotok deck was now filled with fast-tempo Electronic Dance Music (EDM)! Caroline, with headphones draped around her neck, stood near the speaker, posing like a professional DJ at an Ibiza nightclub, not in the middle of the Sekonyer River. She nodded her head following the rhythm, occasionally raising her hand in the air. “Come on everyone! Party on the river! Woohoo! Kalimantan Rave!” she exclaimed.

The others' reactions were varied. Alex immediately joined in swaying a little while recording his aunt's action. Andrea and Sharon laughed with amusement seeing their unpredictable sister's behavior. Reza could only smile with resignation. Nisa? She tried to stay focused on her report folder, but the loud bass thumping made it hard to concentrate. The local boat crew looked at each other in confusion, perhaps wondering whether this was an Irish version of a forest spirit summoning ritual.

But the most epic reaction came from Jim. He immediately lifted his head from his 'Proboscis Monkey Philosophy' book, staring at Caroline with a disturbed gaze. “Caroline! Could you lower the volume of that music… uh… that noise a bit? I'm trying to understand ultrasonic communication patterns between alpha male proboscis monkeys and primiparous females! You're disturbing my research waves!” he protested.
“Come on, Jim! A little music won't hurt the proboscis monkeys!” Caroline replied while continuing to sway. “This makes the forest atmosphere more alive!”
“Alive with noise pollution you mean?” Jim murmured, then tried to focus on his book again, though now with a slightly annoyed expression.
Fortunately, Caroline's 'sudden party' didn't last too long. After three pounding EDM songs, Nisa gave a subtle signal to Reza, who then approached Caroline.
“Car, maybe the music could be changed to something a bit more… merged with nature? Poor Jim is researching proboscis monkeys,” Reza coaxed.

Caroline, who had also begun getting bored, finally agreed. She changed her playlist to calmer chill out ambient music, which was immediately welcomed with a relieved nod from Jim and a grateful smile from Nisa. The klotok atmosphere returned to calm, only the boat engine sound and nature's harmony (minus bass thumping) heard.

The first day's journey along the Sekonyer River closed with a view of dozens of proboscis monkeys with pointed (or flat, depending on Jim's perspective) noses relaxing on tree branches at the river's edge at dusk. A unique and very Kalimantan sight. Jim was of course most enthusiastic, observing them through binoculars while continuing to make notes in his 'sacred' book. Andrea admitted that those proboscis monkeys, though their noses were strange, turned out to be quite adorable and (most importantly) didn't look like they wanted to attack her.

That night, they anchored in the middle of the river, far from settlements. Dinner was served on the upper deck under the dim light of oil lamps and starlight. The atmosphere was so magical and peaceful, only forest night sounds as backdrop. Conversation flowed lightly, sharing impressions about the first day on the klotok, from proboscis monkey philosophy to Caroline's impromptu DJ set. Kalimantan began showing its wild yet soothing charm.
14: The sixteenth day continued with the klotok journey deeper into the heart of Tanjung Puting National Park. Morning on the river felt so magical. Thin mist still blanketed the water surface, sunlight began piercing through dense foliage creating golden ray patterns, and morning bird sounds formed a natural orchestra far more beautiful than any concert.

Breakfast on the upper deck was accompanied by that view. Fried rice, sunny-side-up eggs, crackers, and Kalimantan coffee whose aroma was strong. Andrea, who yesterday was still slightly tense, now looked more relaxed, even enjoying observing the small monkeys playing on the riverbank trees.
“This place is truly… wow,” she said while sipping her coffee. “The atmosphere is so peaceful. Different from Bali, different from Sumba. This is like… entering the earth's lungs.”
“A fitting analogy, Andrea,” Nisa answered while smiling. “Kalimantan's tropical rainforest is indeed one of the world's most important lungs. Its biodiversity is extraordinary.”

Jim, who had returned to his favorite spot with his 'Proboscis Monkey Philosophy' book, chimed in without lifting his head, “And it's precisely that lung whose breath is increasingly shortened by illegal logging and palm oil plantation expansion. A tragic irony of the modern era.” That comment successfully created a brief silence, reminding everyone of the environmental issues behind that beauty.
To break that slightly heavy atmosphere, Reza changed the topic. “So, today's agenda is a bit heavier, everyone. Prepare your feet for a bit of jungle trekking!”

“Trekking? Into the forest? On foot?” Caroline asked, her eyes widening. “There are no clear paths, right? What if we get lost like in Gili Meno? But this time it's not goats we meet, but wild boars or… tigers?”
“There are no tigers in Kalimantan, Caroline,” Alex explained while grinning. “But there might be clouded leopards. Or sun bears. Or…”
“ENOUGH! Don't continue!” Andrea cut him off in panic, immediately checking her handbag contents (probably looking for anti-bear spray she didn't have).

Nisa hurried to calm them. “Relax. We'll be escorted by very experienced local guides. The route we take is a safe official route to Camp Leakey. Along the way we might see various types of trees, orchids, insects, and if lucky, wild orangutans in their natural habitat.”

After preparing themselves (wearing boots, long pants, long-sleeved shirts, hats, and applying anti-insect lotion thickly per Nisa's briefing), the group descended from the klotok at a small dock. Two experienced local guides, Pak Anwar and Bang Udin, were already waiting with warm smiles and machetes tucked at their waists (which made Andrea slightly nervous).

Jungle trekking began. The path was fairly clear but damp and slippery in places, requiring careful walking. Enormous trees towered with their canopies covering the sky, creating a dim yet cool atmosphere. Various sounds were heard: insect chirps, distant bird calls, rustling leaves stepped on.
“This feels like a scene from a Jurassic Park film,” Sharon whispered in amazement, staring at a fern much taller than herself.

Pak Anwar and Bang Udin explained various things along the way. About the ironwood tree whose wood was extraordinarily hard, about ancient rattan vines, about the wild orchid species blooming on tree trunks, and about the traces of animals they passed.
Suddenly, Bang Udin who was walking in front stopped and raised his hand, signaling everyone to be silent. He pointed toward a tall tree not far from them.

There, among the branches and leaves, a large orangutan with thick reddish fur sat calmly eating fruit. That animal looked so majestic and calm, its intelligent eyes occasionally glancing at the group of humans watching it from below.
“Oh… my… God…” Caroline whispered, her mouth agape. “It's so big! And handsome!”
“Wait, is it 'he' or 'she'?” Andrea asked in a whisper.
“That's an adult female orangutan, Ma'am,” Pak Anwar explained in a soft voice. “They usually live alone or with their still-small young.”

They observed that orangutan for several minutes in awe-filled silence. There was no drama, no panic. Only pure amazement at nature's greatness. Even Jim, who was usually full of theories, only stood silently observing with an admiring gaze.

Continuing the journey, they arrived at Camp Leakey, an orangutan research and rehabilitation center that has been operating for decades. There, they were welcomed by center staff and got an explanation about orangutan conservation efforts, the challenges faced (habitat loss, illegal hunting), and the rehabilitation program for orangutans that were once victims of illegal trade.

The visit's highlight was witnessing the supplementary feeding session at a feeding platform in the forest. One by one, semi-wild orangutans of various ages emerged from the forest, hanging on ropes or tree branches, approaching that platform to take bananas and milk provided.

That sight was extraordinarily touching. There were mother orangutans carrying their young, playful young orangutans, and large adult male orangutans with distinctive cheek pads (fatty cheeks) commanding respect.
But then, an incident occurred that would become Andrea's story for years to come.

One young female orangutan, apparently very curious, approached the visitor viewing area boundary. Her eyes stared intently at Andrea, who at that moment happened to be standing at the front row, her long blond hair gleaming caught by sunlight piercing the foliage.
That orangutan tilted her head, seeming enchanted by that unusual hair color. Slowly, she extended her long hairy hand through the fence's gap, trying to reach Andrea's hair.
“UH OH! WHAT IS SHE DOING?!” Andrea shrieked in panic, immediately retreating a few steps while covering her hair with both hands. “SHE WANTS TO PULL MY HAIR! SHE WANTS TO MAKE MY HAIR HER NEST!”

Camp Leakey staff hurriedly stepped in calmly, gently directing that orangutan back to the feeding platform with the lure of a banana. That orangutan finally moved away, though she still occasionally glanced curiously toward Andrea's hair.
“Relax, Ma'am,” one staff member explained while smiling. “She's just curious. Blond hair is rarely seen here. She probably thought it was some kind of unique fruit or dried leaves.”
“Unique fruit?! My hair isn't fruit! This is the result of expensive treatment at a Dublin salon!” Andrea protested, still trembling slightly, but relieved because her hair was safe.
Everyone laughed with amusement seeing that incident. Nisa patted Andrea's shoulder. “Well, at least you now know your hair is attractive not only to humans, but also to primates, Andrea.”
“That's not a compliment, Nisa!” Andrea replied, but she couldn't hold back her own laughter.

Jim, of course, had his own perspective. “Interesting. This shows a high level of curiosity and adaptability in Pongo pygmaeus. She sees an unfamiliar visual stimulus and tries to investigate it directly through the sense of touch. A classic manifestation of empirical scientific method in the primate world.”
“Or she just wanted to steal my shampoo,” Andrea murmured.

Their visit to Camp Leakey closed with an educational discussion session with the researchers there. The Corrs listened attentively about the challenges of orangutan conservation and how the public can contribute. This experience truly opened their eyes, no longer merely enjoying nature's beauty, but also understanding the responsibility to protect it.

Returning to the klotok as afternoon fell, the atmosphere on the deck felt more contemplative. Kalimantan's forest not only presented adventure and silliness, but also profound lessons about the fragility of our shared home. And of course, a funny story about a curious orangutan and Irish blond hair that would surely be retold in Dublin later.
15: Leaving the mystical silence of Kalimantan's rainforest felt like waking from a beautiful yet slightly eerie dream. The Corrs brought home unforgettable memories about majestic orangutans, philosophical proboscis monkeys, and of course, Andrea's paranoia about leeches that fortunately never materialized.

The next destination was a drastic contrast: Derawan Islands in East Kalimantan. If Tanjung Puting was about dense green forest and brownish rivers, Derawan promised turquoise blue seawater so clear, powdery white sand, and an underwater world considered one of the world's best.
The journey from Pangkalan Bun to Berau (Derawan's gateway) required a flight transit, then continued with a fast speedboat cutting through the calm sea for about half an hour.

“WOW! LOOK AT THAT COLOR!” Caroline shrieked as the boat approached Derawan Island. The seawater displayed an unbelievable color gradation: dark blue in deep parts, turquoise green in shallow parts, and nearly transparent near the shore. “That's like… like a Photoshop filter, but real!”
“Insane! Am I dreaming?” Sharon whispered, her eyes not blinking staring at the water's beauty.
Andrea was also transfixed, momentarily forgetting her fear of marine creatures. “This… this is the most beautiful sea I've ever seen. Even more beautiful than the Mediterranean!”

Their lodging in Derawan was a beautiful complex of overwater cottages, wooden houses built above sea water with direct sea access from the terrace stairs. Fish of various types could be seen swimming lazily beneath their cottage floors.
“This is… the coolest natural aquarium in the world!” Alex exclaimed while immediately taking out his fishing rod (which he was later forbidden to use).

That day's main agenda: snorkeling and diving in the famous Derawan waters. Their main targets: green turtles freely swimming around the island, and if lucky, sighting whale sharks (though this was rarer).
Nisa gave a briefing (again) about safety and the importance of not touching coral or marine biota. She also reminded, specifically, about the importance of using sunblock periodically.

“Remember, Derawan's sun is extremely hot,” Nisa emphasized while looking at each Corr member. “Especially for those with fair skin like all of you. Wear sunblock with high SPF, apply evenly, and reapply every two hours or after coming out of the water. Understood?”
“Understood, Madam President!” The Corrs answered in unison, though Nisa slightly doubted the level of their focus (especially Caroline who was already busy testing her fins).

The first snorkeling session went extraordinarily. As soon as their heads entered the water, an underwater paradise unfolded. Colorful coral reefs, thousands of tropical fish of unusual shapes and colors, sea anemones swaying gently. And of course, sea turtles! Dozens of green turtles of various sizes swam calmly around them, some eating seaweed, some resting on coral, some swimming gracefully as if greeting.
“OH MY GOD! TURTLES! SO MANY! THEY'RE SO CUTE!” Caroline shrieked in the water (which of course only came out as bubbles).

Sharon and Andrea were also enchanted. This time, no one panicked. They swam slowly, respecting those turtles' space, enjoying that magical moment. Jim, even with his duck float (which he now considered a “portable observation platform”), tried to observe the turtles' swimming patterns and their possible relationship with earth's magnetic fields.
Nisa and Reza swam side by side, holding hands underwater, sharing amazement at that natural beauty. Alex was busy taking underwater photos with his action camera.

Enthusiasm made them forget time. Hours passed as they explored coral reefs and 'played' with turtles. And here's the problem. In that overflowing enthusiasm, someone forgot Nisa's most important instruction.

Caroline Corr, who was indeed most excited and last out of the water, apparently only applied sunblock once at the beginning, and forgot to reapply. Plus, she spent much time floating on her back on the water surface, sunbathing while resting, without realizing Derawan's sun was mercilessly baking her fair skin.
When they finally returned to the cottage that afternoon, the disaster's results were clearly visible.
“CAROLINE! OH MY GOD! YOUR SKIN!” Andrea shrieked in horror seeing her sister.

Caroline's face, neck, shoulders, and back were bright red like a boiled lobster. It wasn't just red, but a very sharp and even red, especially on her cheeks and nose, contrasting with her still-pale forehead (protected by a hat) and her white eye area (protected by goggles). She looked like… well…

“Goodness, Car! You look like the Irish flag!” Sharon exclaimed, between concerned and holding back laughter. “Green on your bikini top, white on your forehead and around your eyes, orange… uh, bright red on your cheeks and shoulders!”
Caroline stared at herself in the cottage mirror. She was silent momentarily, then… “AAAARGH! HOT! STINGS! WHAT IS THIS?!” she screamed hysterically, feeling the burning pain beginning to sting.
Nisa immediately came, followed by the medical team always on standby. “Caroline! You forgot to reapply sunblock, didn't you?” Nisa asked, her tone mixing concern and slight annoyance.
“I… I forgot, Nisa! The turtles were too cute! I couldn't stop looking at them!” Caroline answered, wincing in pain.

“This is severe sunburn,” the Palace doctor accompanying them said after examining. “Need immediate treatment. Cold compress, aloe vera gel, and pain relief lotion. And absolutely no direct sun exposure for the next few days.”
“NO SUN?! BUT WE'RE ON A TROPICAL ISLAND!” Caroline complained.
“It's your own fault, Car,” Andrea said while helping apply aloe vera gel to her sister's back (accompanied by Caroline's screams every time it was touched). “Nisa reminded us a thousand times.”

That evening turned into a “sunburn nursing session” for Caroline. She had to lie on her stomach on the bed, her body full of cold compresses and green gel, complaining every few minutes about the burning pain. The Corrs and Nisa's family took turns accompanying and (occasionally) laughing at her Irish flag appearance.

Jim, of course, had a scientific analysis. “Ultraviolet B rays from sunlight damage the DNA in your skin cells, Caroline, triggering an inflammatory response as a defense mechanism. Well, that's what causes the redness and pain. Actually, this is proof your immune system is working actively.”
“I don't want to hear about my immune system, Jim! I want ice cream! Lots of ice cream! To cool my body from inside!” Caroline whined.

Fortunately, the cottage's kitchen had plenty of ice cream stock. That night, they all sat on the overwater terrace, watching a spectacular sunset above Derawan's sea, while enjoying ice cream. Caroline lay on a lounge chair, still red-hot but somewhat calmer after taking pain medication and consuming three scoops of chocolate ice cream.
“See that sky's color?” Sharon said while pointing at the sunset. “Orange and pink. Almost the same as your cheek color earlier, Car.”
Caroline threw an ice cream spoon at her sister. “Shut up, Sharon!”

That day, the beauty of Derawan's underwater world presented an unforgettable experience. But Caroline's carelessness in reapplying sunblock also presented a valuable lesson (and a very painful one). At least, they now had a new nickname for Caroline: “The Irish Flag of Derawan.” And Andrea? She promised to bring five bottles of sunblock for the next trip.
16: The twentieth morning in Derawan was welcomed with a more… calm atmosphere. The main reason? Caroline Corr was still in “intensive care” status because of her severe sunburn. She lay on a lounge chair on the cottage's shaded terrace, wearing an oversized T-shirt (the only clothing that didn't hurt when touching her skin), her face still bright red, and surrounded by aloe vera gel bottles, cold compresses, and of course, a glass of iced tea.
“How do you feel, Car?” Nisa asked while approaching, bringing a plate of fresh fruit.
“Like I'm being fried alive,” Caroline answered dramatically, without lifting her head. “But a bit better than yesterday. At least now I can move without screaming.”
“Good. Today, the schedule for you is total rest. No sun, no seawater. Understood?”
“Yes, Madam President Nurse,” Caroline answered while giving a lazy salute.

Because Caroline couldn't join water activities, Nisa changed that day's agenda. Instead of continuing snorkeling to Kakaban or Sangalaki island, they would do a cultural activity on land that could be enjoyed by everyone (including patients under solar treatment): learning Dayak dance!
“Dance? Dayak dance?” Andrea repeated, her eyebrow rising. “Is that… the war dance with axes?”

“There are various types, Andrea,” Nisa explained while smiling. “Today we'll learn a welcome dance or Gantar dance, which is calmer, using bamboo and grain as props. Symbolizing joy and gratitude for a good harvest.”
“Oh, so no axes? Thank God,” Andrea sighed in relief.

A team of professional Dayak dancers from a nearby village had been specially invited to the cottage's spacious open pavilion. Their traditional clothing was so beautiful: colorful cloth with intricate embroidery, headdresses adorned with hornbill feathers, and beaded accessories that jingled with every movement.

Ibu Lastri, a senior dancer with an authoritative yet friendly aura, would be their instructor. She explained briefly about that dance's philosophy, then began demonstrating the basic movements: soft footsteps, hand movements holding bamboo and grain rhythmically, and head and body movements that gently followed the music.
“This dance emphasizes harmony and gracefulness,” Ibu Lastri explained through a translator. “Its movements aren't too fast, but must be full of feeling and rhythmically precise.”
“Okay, sounds easy,” Andrea said confidently.
But apparently, “looking easy” and “doing easily” are two very different things. The practice session began, accompanied by live sape (Dayak traditional stringed instrument) and gong music.

Nisa and Reza, who had indeed occasionally learned regional dances for state events, could follow the basic movements fairly well, though not perfectly. Alex, with his teenage body still flexible, was also quite quick at learning.

Sharon Corr, with her violinist's soul very sensitive to rhythm and body precision, turned out to be the fastest and most graceful learner. Her movements were flowing, her hand placements precise, and her expression looked calm and appreciative. Ibu Lastri even praised her several times. “Very good, Mbak Sharon! Your feeling is there!”

Jim Corr? Ah, Jim. He tried very hard. But his tall thin body and stiff movements made him look… well, like a scarecrow trying to dance. His footsteps didn't sync with the music, his hands holding the bamboo looked awkward, and his face was very serious, full of concentration trying to remember the movement sequence.
“Jim, relax your body a bit,” Ibu Lastri directed patiently. “Don't be too stiff. Let it flow following the music.”
“I'm trying, Ibu Lastri,” Jim answered while wiping sweat. “But my brain keeps trying to calculate the angle of my elbow bend and the frequency of my footsteps for maximum efficiency of movement.”
“Just don't calculate, Jim! Just feel!” Sharon exclaimed while laughing at her brother's behavior.

And Andrea Corr? She was the opposite of Jim. Instead of being stiff, she was… too much. Her enthusiasm to look graceful and appreciate that culture made her exaggerate every movement. Her footsteps were too wide like walking on a fashion catwalk. Her hand movements were too flourishing like an opera diva. Her facial expression was too dramatic, sometimes closing her eyes with a devout style, sometimes smiling too widely.
“Andrea, this isn't a solo Broadway performance,” Nisa admonished while holding back laughter. “This is group dance emphasizing harmony.”
“But I'm trying to convey the joy of harvest, Nisa!” Andrea replied while continuing her extra movements. “This is total artistic expression!”
Ibu Lastri could only smile with resignation seeing her two 'extreme' students. “It's alright,” she said gently. “The important thing is spirit and willingness to learn.”
Caroline, watching from her lounge chair on the terrace, became the loudest commentator (though her voice was still slightly hoarse).
“Jim! Your body is like a broken robot!” she shouted, laughing.
“Andrea! Are you being possessed by a rice spirit?!” she teased again.
“Sharon! You're so cool! Ready to compete at the Dayak Dance World Cup!”

Because she couldn't join in, Caroline appointed herself “official commentator” and “head judge” of that dance practice session. She even gave scores to each participant with the style of a Dancing with the Stars program judge.
“Okay! Score for Sharon: 9.5! Nearly perfect, just needs a bit more hip movement!”
“Score for Nisa and Reza: 8! Good, but seems still burdened by state affairs!”
“Score for Alex: 7.5! Talented, but a bit lazy!”
“Score for Jim: 4! Sorry, Bro, but your movements are more suitable for a mathematics theory presentation than a harvest dance!”
“And score for Andrea: 6! Full of spirit, but too extra! Remember, An, less is more!”
Everyone laughed hearing Caroline's judgment. That dance practice session finally turned into a very entertaining event, complete with unofficial commentary and judgment from the sunburn patient.

At the session's end, Ibu Lastri and her team performed the complete Gantar dance perfectly, making everyone applaud in admiration. The Corrs then tried performing it together (with results that could still be called chaotic but full of laughter), accompanied by Caroline who tried tapping the rhythm with her hand on the lounge chair's edge.

That day, though colored by Caroline's whining and Jim's stiff and Andrea's extra movements, became another unforgettable day. They not only learned about the beauty of Dayak dance, but also about accepting each other's limitations (and silliness). And Caroline? She swore that as soon as her skin healed, she would prove that she could dance far better than Jim and Andrea combined.
17: After several days in Kalimantan's tropical paradise (which ended with the Derawan sunburn drama and the chaotic Dayak dance), the group headed toward the next destination: Sumatra! Their first target was North Sumatra, the land of the Batak with its magnificent Lake Toba, cool mountain air, and of course, distinctive culinary that would again test The Corrs' tongues.

The flight to Silangit or Kualanamu, then land journey to the Lake Toba area, presented a very different atmosphere. Green pine hills, cool air (making Andrea rummage for her scarf again), and view of the world's largest volcanic lake stretching so vast it resembled a sea.
“WOW! Is this really a lake? It's like the sea!” Sharon exclaimed as their car passed the road along the lake's edge.

“Correct. This is Lake Toba, the world's largest volcanic lake, resulting from a super volcano eruption tens of thousands of years ago,” Nisa explained. “And that island in its middle is Samosir Island.”

Jim immediately went into research mode. “A super volcano eruption? That means there's massive geological energy potential still stored beneath us? Is there active monitoring for possible future eruptions? Or…” he lowered his voice, “…is this eruption caldera actually an ancient alien base cleverly disguised?”
“Jim, please, don't start again,” Andrea murmured.

Their lodging was a beautiful boutique hotel on Samosir Island's edge, with cottages in traditional Batak architectural style but modern facilities, facing directly onto the calm lake. The atmosphere was so peaceful, only the sound of gentle waves lapping and the whistle of pine trees heard.

That day was spent enjoying Lake Toba's tranquility. They tried canoeing on the lake's edge, cycling around the village on Samosir Island, or simply sitting relaxed on the cottage terrace, admiring the view.

Caroline, whose sunburn had begun to heal (though her skin was starting to peel like a snake shedding), finally could join activities again, though still cautious about sun exposure. She looked most enthusiastic being able to move freely again.

That evening, that day's culinary highlight arrived. Nisa had specially ordered Lake Toba's most famous specialty dish: Arsik Fish, or Naniura, or… the more challenging one: Batak Pork Grill (of course prepared separately and with clear labeling, respecting religious differences within the group). But the main star, and the one considered the biggest challenge, was Batak Andaliman Sauce.

“So, tonight we'll try some authentic Batak dishes,” Nisa announced with an anticipation-filled smile. “There's arsik fish (goldfish cooked with distinctive Batak seasonings), lake grilled fish, and boiled cassava leaves. And of course, its inseparable companion: andaliman sauce.”
“Andaliman? What's that?” Andrea asked, sniffing the food aroma beginning to be served, which smelled fragrant, sour, and slightly… numbing?

“Andaliman is a distinctive Batak spice, sometimes called Batak pepper or Szechuan pepper,” Reza explained. “Its taste is unique. Slightly spicy, fragrantly citrus, but its most distinctive sensation is… numbing? Tingling on the tongue?”
“Numbing? Tingling?” Caroline repeated, her eyes gleaming curiously. “Like electric shock? Cool!”
“Kind of,” Nisa answered while laughing. “But not painful. It's more like… tingling. And it makes food taste more delicious.”
Dinner began. Andaliman sauce was served in a small bowl, its color reddish-green with tiny grains scattered within (the andaliman itself). Its aroma was strong, fragrantly sour.
Sharon was the first to dare taste it. She took a bit of that sauce with a spoon, then put it in her mouth. Her expression instantly changed. Her eyes widened, her lips slightly parted.

“Oh! This… this is interesting!” she said while trying to identify the sensation. “Spicy, yes. Sour, yes. But there's something else… my tongue feels… vibrating? Tingling? This is truly a unique sensation!”
Andrea, seeing her sister's reaction, hesitated. But her curiosity was greater. She took a bit of that sauce (very little), then put it in her mouth.
Three… two… one…

“AAAAAAH! MY TONGUE! MY TONGUE IS PARALYZED! ELECTRIC! WHAT'S IN THIS?!” Andrea shrieked while immediately grabbing a glass of water and drinking it in one gulp. “It's not spicy! But it's… STRANGE! My tongue can't feel anything anymore! Am I poisoned?!”
Everyone laughed at Andrea's reaction. “That's the andaliman sensation, Andrea!” Nisa exclaimed while wiping away tears from laughing. “That's normal! It'll disappear on its own in a few minutes.”
“NORMAL?! I feel like I got dental anesthesia in my entire mouth!” Andrea protested, still fanning her tongue.

Jim, of course, immediately took his notebook. “This is very interesting! This numbing sensation is caused by the compound hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, which activates the touch and vibration receptors in the mouth, not the pain receptors like capsaicin in chili. So, this is a tactile, not thermal sensation!” he explained enthusiastically. “This has enormous potential for use in developing new anesthesia techniques or even revolutionizing molecular gastronomy!”
“Jim, please, just enjoy the food,” Sharon said while shaking her head.

Caroline, who was indeed most adventurous with taste, took quite a bit of that andaliman sauce and mixed it with her rice and arsik fish. “Come on, tongue! Give me your best electric shock!” she exclaimed before eating it.

Her reaction? She fell silent momentarily, chewing slowly, her eyes widening. Then… “AAAH! THIS IS AMAZING! MY TONGUE IS DANCING! THIS IS LIKE A PARTY IN MY MOUTH! I LOVE ANDALIMAN!” she screamed enthusiastically, immediately taking more sauce.

Nisa and Reza looked at each other, amazed at the diversity of reactions to one spice. Sharon appreciated its uniqueness, Andrea was traumatized, Jim was scientifically fascinated, and Caroline instantly became a fan.

Besides andaliman, other Batak dishes also received varied responses. The arsik fish with its thick distinctive seasoning was praised by Sharon and Nisa. The lake grilled fish was liked by everyone because of its fresh sweet taste. The boiled cassava leaves? Andrea asked whether this was grass mistakenly cooked.

That night, Lake Toba's culinary experience became one of the most memorable in their journey. Not because of overflowing luxury, but because of the authenticity of taste and unique sensations they'd never felt before. And of course, because of Andrea's dramatic reaction to andaliman that would surely be remembered for a long time.

After dinner, they sat relaxed on the cottage terrace, gazing at the calm Lake Toba illuminated by moonlight. The cool air made them hug their jackets closer. Sharon took out her violin and played a soft melody inspired by the lake's atmosphere. Caroline hummed following her rhythm. Jim was busy noting his hypothesis about andaliman's future in the pharmaceutical world.

That serene atmosphere felt so perfect. Sumatra had welcomed them with its natural beauty and “electrifying” culinary. What silliness awaited them in the next few days? Perhaps a durian eating contest? Nisa smiled at the thought.
18: Leaving Kalimantan with all its forest and river charm felt like closing a chapter full of wild adventure. Now, the (presidential, of course) plane's wheels carried Nisa's group and The Corrs toward Indonesia's westernmost island: Sumatra. Their first destination was one of the world's most spectacular natural wonders: Lake Toba in North Sumatra, Southeast Asia's largest volcanic lake.

The flight to the airport was filled with The Corrs trying to guess what Lake Toba would be like. “So, this is the lake formed from a super massive volcanic eruption thousands of years ago?” Sharon asked, her eyes gleaming curiously. “I read in Nisa's guidebook, its eruption nearly wiped out humanity!”

“Technically, yes,” Jim chimed in, who had surely read the same chapter (or perhaps a thicker geology book). “The Ancient Toba eruption was one of the largest supervolcano events in earth's history. The energy released was equivalent to thousands of atomic bombs. Interesting to imagine its impact on Homo sapiens evolution at that time.”
“What matters is the lake is safe now, right, Nisa?” Andrea asked anxiously. “No potential for erupting again anytime soon? Or suddenly a lake monster emerging from the crater floor?”
Nisa laughed. “Safe, Andrea. Now the lake is very calm and beautiful. And its monster is at most just a giant goldfish.”

The land journey from the airport toward the Lake Toba area, specifically to Samosir Island located in the lake's middle, took several hours. But the view truly paid it off. Winding roads climbing up and down, passing cool pine forests, green valleys, and finally… the extraordinarily vast Lake Toba view unfolded. Its water was calm blue, surrounded by magnificent green giant caldera walls. In its middle, Samosir Island looked like an emerald green gem.

“This… this isn't a lake! This is an ocean!” Caroline shrieked in amazement seeing Lake Toba for the first time from the Tele viewpoint. “Hard to believe this formed from a volcanic eruption,” Sharon added, truly enchanted.

They crossed to Samosir Island by ferry (the comfortable VVIP version, of course) and headed toward their lodging: a beautiful resort at the lake's edge with modernized Batak Toba traditional house architecture. Each room had a private balcony facing directly onto the lake.

After resting briefly and enjoying lunch with Batak specialty dishes like grilled tilapia and sambal tuktuk (which immediately made Sharon and Nisa compete on spiciness again), Nisa announced the evening agenda.
“Tonight we won't do heavy activities,” Nisa said. “But we'll try feeling one of the Batak people's most favorite entertainments here…”
“What is it? Bullfighting?” Andrea guessed.
“No,” Nisa smiled. “Karaoke!”
“Karaoke?!” The Corrs exclaimed simultaneously. Their faces showed an expression mixing amusement and slight… dread? They were world-class musicians, but karaoke?
“Not ordinary karaoke,” Reza added. “This is Batak Karaoke! The songs are Batak regional songs usually full of spirit and… shrill high notes!”

That night, they were taken to a lapo (traditional Batak eatery or restaurant) near the lodging famous for its relaxed atmosphere and lively karaoke sessions. That place wasn't too large, dominated by wooden furniture, with a small stage in the room's corner and a large TV screen displaying song lyrics. Several locals and domestic tourists were already engrossed in singing by turns when Nisa's group arrived (of course with not-too-conspicuous Presidential Security Force guarding).

Initially The Corrs only sat nicely, enjoying the atmosphere, ordering warm Bandrek (ginger spice drink), and listening to other visitors singing Batak songs with full feeling (and sometimes slightly off-key, but full of confidence). Sounds of laughter, applause, and shouts of “Horas!” were heard everywhere.
Then, the lapo owner, a middle-aged Batak man with a paunch and thundering voice, recognized Nisa (who wouldn't recognize the President?). With full spirit, he immediately went up on stage.

“Horas, Madam President! Horas, our guests from Ireland!” he greeted loudly through the microphone, making all eyes turn to the Palace group's table. “A great honor for our lapo to be visited tonight! As a welcome, how about our guests from Ireland contribute one song?”

All eyes now turned to The Corrs. Andrea immediately shook her head in panic. Jim pretended to be busy reading the menu (again). Caroline bowed holding back a smile. That left Sharon, the calmest and fastest at adapting.
“Come on, Sharon!” Nisa whispered encouragingly. “Just one song! Choose the easiest Batak song!”

With encouragement from Nisa, Reza, Alex, and applause from other visitors, Sharon finally worked up the courage to step onto the stage. The lapo owner enthusiastically helped her choose a fairly popular Batak song whose tempo wasn't too fast, “Anak Medan.” Its lyrics were displayed on the TV screen.
The music began. Sharon took a breath, holding the microphone with slight trembling (something that rarely happened to her). She began to sing…

Her voice was of course melodious as usual. But her Batak accent… sounded very… Irish. Several words were pronounced with funny articulation. There were notes slightly off because they were perhaps foreign to her ear. But she sang it with full feeling and a sincere smile.

The audience in that lapo fell silent momentarily, listening attentively. Then, slowly, smiles began blooming on their faces. They could see Sharon's hard effort, her sincerity in trying to sing their pride song. They might be slightly confused by her Irish-Batak accent, but they also felt… moved.

When the song finished, lively applause immediately thundered throughout the lapo. Not applause because her performance was perfect, but applause of appreciation for her courage and sincerity. Several Batak mothers were even seen wiping the corners of their eyes.
“Horas, Miss! Your voice is so melodious! Your accent is unique!” shouted the lapo owner from below the stage while giving two thumbs up.
Sharon returned to the table with a reddened face but also a relieved smile. “That… was more nerve-wracking than performing in front of 50 thousand people!” she whispered to Nisa.

That night continued with an increasingly fluid and intimate atmosphere. Andrea, after seeing Sharon 'survive,' worked up the courage to sing The Corrs' own song, “Runaway,” which was immediately welcomed with lively sing-along by nearly all visitors (turns out The Corrs songs were also quite popular among Batak fathers!). Caroline and Alex even managed to duet the newest Indonesian pop song with great commotion. Jim? He remained faithful at his table, this time trying to analyze the melodic and harmonic structure of the Batak songs he heard.

Batak Karaoke that night became an unforgettable cultural experience. They not only enjoyed music, but also directly felt the warmth and spirit of togetherness of the Batak Toba people. And Sharon? She might never forget the moment when her Irish-Batak accent successfully made locals moved and confused at once.
19: The twenty-third morning on Samosir Island was welcomed with thin mist blanketing Lake Toba's surface, creating a peaceful mystical atmosphere. Remnants of last night's Batak Karaoke festivity might still be slightly felt (especially in Sharon's throat which was somewhat hoarse from trying the Batak song's high notes), but the spirit to explore Toba culture more deeply remained burning.

After a delicious Medan lontong sayur breakfast (Caroline immediately asked the hotel chef for the recipe) and enjoying the lake view from the room terrace, Nisa announced that day's main agenda: “Today we'll try becoming Batak chefs! We'll learn to cook one of the most iconic and philosophy-filled dishes from Toba land: Arsik Ikan Mas!”

A semi-traditional open kitchen with a direct lake view had been prepared in the resort area. An inang (respectful term for mother in Batak language) named Inang Rosida, famous as one of Samosir's best Arsik cooks, was already waiting with a friendly smile and a pile of fresh ingredients that looked exotic to The Corrs.

On the long table, fresh fairly large goldfish were lined up (which made Andrea wince slightly), various aromatic reddish-yellow seasonings, long beans, Medan eggplant, lokio (Batak onion), and two key spices that most intrigued The Corrs: Andaliman (Batak pepper with a bitter and slightly 'numbing' sensation on the tongue) and Kecombrang/Rias flower (pink flower with a sharp and fresh distinctive aroma).

“This Arsik isn't merely ordinary cooking for us Batak people, sir and ma'am,” Inang Rosida began her explanation with a thick Batak accent. “This is a mandatory dish at important traditional events, symbolizing prayer and good hope. The goldfish must be whole from head to tail, its scales not all removed, symbolizing a whole and perfect life. Its rich spice seasoning symbolizes diversity that unites.”
The Corrs listened with full interest. Even Jim looked serious absorbing the philosophical explanation behind that dish.

First stage: cleaning and preparing the goldfish. This was the most challenging part for Andrea. Seeing a whole goldfish with its eyes still 'staring,' she immediately retreated several steps. “I… I can't! He's like still alive!” she shrieked. “Andrea, the fish is already dead,” Sharon said trying to calm her. “Just think of him as taking a long nap.” Finally, with help from Alex who bravely (though also slightly squeamish) held the fish, Andrea worked up the courage to help clean the fish's insides (while closing her eyes). Caroline was instead more interested in the gleaming fish scales. “Can these scales be made into glitter for stage costumes?”

Second stage: Grinding the seasoning. Inang Rosida showed how to use a traditional stone grinder and also a mortar. Remembering the 'trauma' of grinding Ayam Taliwang seasoning, this time The Corrs preferred trying the stone grinder. Jim, with his mechanic's soul, was immediately interested in that tool's working mechanism. Sharon and Caroline took turns grinding, exerting a bit of extra strength. Andrea's task was adding seasoning bit by bit (while making sure her hands didn't touch chili). The distinctive aroma of andaliman and kecombrang began wafting, making their noses slightly 'tickled.'

While observing the goldfish already lying neatly inside the wok, ready to be cooked, Jim Corr suddenly approached, staring at that fish intently. He noticed the goldfish's scales gleaming caught by light. Then, he turned to Inang Rosida and asked in his characteristic serious tone.

“Inang Rosida, this goldfish's scales are so beautiful, gleaming like… like mini piano keys,” Jim began, making the others exchange glances, already guessing where this conversation was heading. “Is there… is there a possibility this goldfish, besides being delicious cooked as Arsik, actually also has hidden musical talent? I mean, could these scales produce notes if touched in a certain way? Or maybe this fish could hum Lake Toba's ancient melody if we listen to it carefully?”

Jim's question instantly made the atmosphere fall silent momentarily. Inang Rosida blinked her eyes, appearing confused about what to answer. Nisa held back laughter until her stomach hurt. Reza covered his face with both hands. Alex hurriedly recorded Inang Rosida's confused expression.

“This gentleman… what an imagination!” Inang Rosida said finally while smiling with amusement. “As far as I know, this goldfish when cooked as Arsik, its most melodious sound is in the stomach, sir. Never heard him play music.”

“Ah, what a shame,” Jim murmured, appearing slightly disappointed because his hypothesis wasn't proven. “And I had already imagined a collaboration between Sharon's violin and a 'goldfish scale orchestra.'”
Laughter then exploded in that open kitchen. Jim's absurd question successfully melted the tense atmosphere while waiting for the Arsik to cook.

The Arsik cooking process took quite a long time, because it had to be cooked over low heat until the water reduced and the seasoning absorbed perfectly, without stirring so the fish wouldn't fall apart. While waiting, Nisa took The Corrs for a relaxed walk around the resort. Jim used that time to write notes about 'the musical potential of volcanic freshwater fauna.'

Finally, that Arsik Ikan Mas was cooked. Its aroma was extraordinarily fragrant, a blend between savory fish, spicy-bitter andaliman, fresh sour kecombrang, and various other spices. Its color was appetizingly reddish-yellow.

Time to taste. The goldfish's flesh was so tender, its seasoning absorbed down to the bone. The spicy-bitter taste of andaliman gave a unique small 'electric' sensation on the tongue, blending perfectly with the fresh sourness of kecombrang and the savoriness of the yellow seasoning.

“THIS… THIS IS EXTRAORDINARY!” Sharon exclaimed after the first bite. “The taste is so complex! I've never tasted anything like this!” “I like this 'numbing' sensation from the andaliman!” Caroline added enthusiastically. “Like there's a small electric shock that's addictive!” Even Jim looked to so enjoy it that he forgot to analyze.

Learning to cook Arsik Ikan Mas became a very memorable culinary and cultural experience for The Corrs. They not only learned a new recipe, but also understood the philosophy behind it. And of course, they gained one more funny story about Jim Corr's magical question involving goldfish and music.
The twenty-third day at Lake Toba closed with full stomachs, happy hearts, and tongues still slightly 'numb' from andaliman.
20: The twenty-fourth day on Samosir presented a Lake Toba view so clear and calm in the morning. The thin mist that had blanketed the lake last night was gone, replaced by clear North Sumatra blue sky and sunlight reflecting off the vast boundless lake surface. The air felt fresh and slightly cool, perfect for starting the day.

After a Mie Gomak breakfast (which made Caroline ask whether this was Batak-version spaghetti) and hearty Sidikalang coffee (Jim immediately noted its flavor profile to compare with the Gayo coffee he'd once tried), Nisa felt a rare desire: a bit of time alone with Reza.

Throughout more than three weeks of this journey, though very enjoyable and full of laughter with The Corrs, their private moments as a couple had been nearly nonexistent. There was always a schedule, always a group, always the Presidential Security Force (though keeping distance), and of course, always Alex ready with his camera or drone.

“Mas,” Nisa whispered to Reza as they relaxed briefly on the room balcony facing the lake, while the other Corrs were engrossed trying to play Batak chess with Alex (who lost more often because Caroline kept disturbing him). “I saw in this resort's brochure there are kayak facilities. How about we try briefly? Just the two of us?”

Reza turned, a smile immediately blooming on his face. He knew exactly what his wife wanted. A quiet moment, far from the crowd, just the two of them amid Lake Toba's beauty. A luxury they greatly missed. “Great idea, Darling,” he answered gently, gripping Nisa's hand. “It's been so long since we did something slightly… romantic like this.”

They then quietly (or at least tried to look inconspicuous) asked permission from the security team and prepared two brightly colored single kayaks. Nisa made sure her phone was on silent mode and didn't bring any work folders. Reza left all his business matters in the room. This was their time.

Kayaking on Lake Toba's calm waters turned out to be easier than imagined. The water was clear, the wind gentle. They paddled slowly away from the resort's edge, toward a quieter part of the lake, accompanied only by the sound of water splashing from paddles.

“So beautiful, isn't it, Mas,” Nisa said softly, stopping her paddling briefly, letting her kayak float calmly. She closed her eyes, feeling the warmth of morning sunlight and the peace enveloping her.

“Very beautiful,” Reza replied, also stopping paddling near Nisa. He wasn't looking at the lake view, but at Nisa's face which looked so peaceful and happy, free from the furrowed brow of thinking about the state. “But not as beautiful as you when you smile freely like this.”
Nisa's cheeks reddened slightly. “Ah, you always say something,” she said shyly, a reaction rarely seen from her in public.
They chatted lightly, about Alex's college plans, about Reza's dream of opening a small art gallery, about the last romantic comedy film they watched. Such a rare and precious moment.
While engrossed in reminiscing hand in hand (rather difficult to do atop a swaying kayak, but they managed), suddenly a familiar buzzing sound was heard from above.
Bzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzt…
Nisa and Reza looked at each other. “Don't tell me that's…” Nisa murmured, her feeling beginning to turn uneasy.
And sure enough. A small white drone flew closer, hovering right above their kayak, its camera clearly aimed at them.
“ALEXANDER DAMAR SATRIA!” Nisa shouted toward land (though she knew Alex might not hear her from that distance). Her peaceful face immediately changed slightly annoyed. Her romantic moment disturbed!
That drone flew lower, as if wanting to get a close-up of their expressions. Reza tried to shoo it with a wave of his paddle. “Hussh! Hussh! Go away!”
That drone dodged slightly, then returned again, this time flying in circles around their kayak like a giant mischievous mosquito.
“That child, really!” Nisa grumbled, between annoyed and amused. “Parents' privacy on a date, disturbed using technology.”
“Maybe he wants to make content 'Romantic But Failed Moment of the President and First Gentleman Because of Their Son's Mischievous Drone'?” Reza joked, trying to melt Nisa's annoyance.
They tried to ignore that drone and continue their romantic conversation, but the buzzing sound and the presence of a flying camera continuously watching truly ruined the atmosphere.
“Enough, Mas,” Nisa said finally, surrendering to that disturbance. “Seems like our 'romantic date' is now officially sponsored by the Palace documentation division, Samosir branch.”
Reza laughed. “Oh well. At least we get free documentation, right?” He then waved toward the drone. “Alex! If you want to record, get a good angle! So Papa looks handsome!”

They finally decided to return to the resort's edge, ending that (disturbed) romantic kayak session earlier than planned. From a distance, they could see The Corrs standing on the small dock, waving while laughing. It seemed they also enjoyed Alex's drone 'drama.'
“You two are like film stars being chased by drone paparazzi!” Caroline exclaimed as Nisa and Reza pulled up to the dock.
“So romantic… until there was a giant bee sound from above,” Andrea added innocently.

Nisa could only shake her head while looking for Alex, ready to give special 'advice' to her only son. Their romantic moment might not have gone smoothly as hoped, but at least, it became one more funny story in the album of memories from their colorful month-long vacation. And Nisa was again reminded, being President and Mother at the same time does need extra patience, especially if your child has a drone and a slightly… mischievous sense of humor.
21: Chapter 25 (Day 25): “Belgica Fort Banda Neira and Caroline's Strange Nutmeg-Clove Perfume” — Exploring the Spice Island

The journey to the Banda Islands in Central Maluku felt like time travel. After the comfort of the presidential plane that brought them from North Sumatra to Ambon, the next journey to Banda Neira felt more 'adventurous.' They boarded a smaller pioneer plane, flying low over blue-green seas decorated with clusters of small volcanic islands looking like scattered emeralds.
“It feels like we're flying to the end of the world,” Sharon whispered to Andrea, her eyes not leaving the plane window.
“The end of the world that hopefully has Wi-Fi signal,” Andrea chimed in, slightly anxious imagining being isolated from civilization (and social media).

As soon as that small plane landed on Banda Neira Airport's simple runway, they were immediately welcomed by warm sea air and a faint yet strongly felt distinctive aroma: a mixture of sweet nutmeg and clove fragrance carried by the wind. The small town of Banda Neira itself looked so calm and enchanting. Old Dutch colonial buildings stood gracefully along narrow streets, as if frozen in history.
Their lodging was a historic guesthouse beautifully renovated, once perhaps a former Dutch official's residence, with a lush garden filled with nutmeg and canary nut trees.

“This place has… a different aura,” Jim said while observing the guesthouse's architecture. “I can feel the layers of history in these walls. Stories about the glory of spices, colonialism, slavery, rebellion…”
“Jim, can we save the history lecture until after we drink young coconut ice first?” Caroline cut in, already hot after getting off the plane.

Their first agenda in Banda Neira was exploring this island's icon: Belgica Fort. This 17th century Dutch colonial fort shaped like a pentagon stood sturdy atop a small hill, facing toward the harbor and Banda Volcano towering gracefully across the sea.

They climbed stone stairs toward the fort's peak. From atop the bastion, the view was truly extraordinary. Blue sea as far as the eye could see, small green islands around it, and the mighty Banda Volcano.

“This is the most beautiful view I've seen during this whole journey!” Andrea exclaimed, momentarily forgetting her worry about Wi-Fi signal. She immediately busied herself taking selfies with Banda Volcano as background.

Jim, of course, was more interested in that fort's architecture and history. He observed the cannon holes and asked a local amateur historian about the battles that had once occurred here. “This pentagonal fort's defense strategy is very interesting. Minimizing blind spots for artillery. Quite advanced 17th century military technology.”

Nisa and Reza stood side by side, enjoying the sea breeze while exchanging stories about Banda's important history in Indonesia's independence struggle (several proclamation figures were once exiled here).

After satisfying themselves exploring Belgica Fort, they were taken to visit one of the nutmeg and clove plantations still managed by locals. Walking beneath the shade of tall nutmeg trees, with their golden-yellow fruits hanging from branches, was a unique experience. The guide explained how this spice's price was once equivalent to gold in Europe.

Caroline looked most enthusiastic at this plantation. She picked several dried clove flowers and sniffed them. She also took several nutmeg fruits that had fallen to the ground. Her eyes gleamed, as if a new idea appeared in her head.
“Nisa, Ma'am Guide,” Caroline suddenly asked. “These clove flowers and nutmeg fruits smell so good, don't they? Could they… be made into perfume?”
The guide smiled. “They could, Miss. Nutmeg oil and clove oil are indeed often base ingredients for perfume or aromatherapy. But the extraction process is complicated, requires distillation.”
But Caroline seemed not to hear the “complicated process” part too much. Her experimental soul (which sometimes ended in disaster, like when cooking Ayam Taliwang) had already stirred.
That afternoon, when they returned to the guesthouse and had free time, Caroline disappeared into her room. Half an hour later, she reappeared with a mysterious smile and a small bottle in her hand.
“Taraaa! I succeeded in making Banda Neira's distinctive perfume!” she exclaimed proudly.
“Wow, that fast?” Sharon asked in wonder. “How?”

“Caroline Corr's kitchen secret!” she answered while laughing. “I just crushed dried clove flowers and a bit of nutmeg seed I took earlier, then mixed it with… ehm… a bit of hand sanitizer from my bag so there'd be alcohol, then I put in frangipani petals so it'd be pretty!”
Nisa and Reza looked at each other, trying to hold back laughter while also slightly horrified imagining that mixture. Jim approached, sniffing the aroma from that bottle carefully.

“Hmm, its aroma is… complex,” Jim commented. “There's a sweet spicy aroma from clove and nutmeg, a bit of synthetic alcohol aroma from the sanitizer, and… a touch of… antiseptic aroma? This is more like a mosquito repellent concoction than perfume, Caroline.”

Andrea worked up the courage to spray a bit of that 'perfume' on her wrist. She sniffed it. Her face immediately furrowed. “Ouch! The smell is… so strange! Like a mixture of spekuk cake spice, medicated oil, and floor cleaner!”
Caroline pouted. “Really? I think its fragrance is exotic!”
“Maybe exotic for an alien's nose, Car,” quipped Alex who had just arrived.
That “Caroline's Strange Nutmeg-Clove Perfume” experiment was officially declared a total failure, yet successfully added one more funny story to their journey.

The first day on that spice island closed with a fresh seafood dinner seasoned with nutmeg and clove (this time authentic seasoning, not Caroline's concoction) at a small beachside restaurant. They enjoyed Banda's calm night atmosphere, while exchanging stories about the fort's history, the nutmeg tree's wonder, and of course, Caroline's failure as an impromptu perfumer.
